title: The last of the rock forests

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In many ways, Mt Eden is a typical residential neighbourhood in the city of Auckland, New Zealand. However, it is also home to a woodland where broadleaf trees grow amongst giant volcanic rocks. The woodland is all that remains from a prehistoric rock forest which once covered over 5,000 hectares, but is now much reduced and split into small areas. One of these areas is the Withiel Thomas Reserve (WTR), occupying 0.7 hectares, and which contains native trees like põhutukawa and titokī. One of the first things visitors observe in the WTR is the way in which tree roots extend and cover the surface of the rocks. Ewen Cameron, curator of botany at Auckland Museum, explains they spread like this because the trees are always searching for water, of which there is very little in the rock forest. This is because the rock forest in the WTR has virtually no soil, just a build-up of old leaves between the many rocks. Although Mt Eden residents may enjoy strolling through the reserve, it is possible that many do not appreciate just how valuable it is to researchers and conservationists.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: A variety of fern, moss and lichen species also help make the WTR a rare habitat; extremely rare in fact. Ecologists previously used the phrase 'historically rare' when referring to ecosystems that were less than 0.5 per cent of the prehistoric landscape. Now they use 'naturally uncommon' instead, which emphasises the development of ecosystems before human activity. It is true, though, that the young nīkau palms growing throughout the WTR are recent additions. Cameron says they were not planted deliberately, and guesses they are here as a result of birds dropping seeds from adult plants growing in nearby gardens, which is a common occurrence.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The WTR is not the only piece of rock forest in Mt Eden; another is a smaller section referred to as the Almorah Road forest. Cameron believes the Almorah Road ecosystem has not been disturbed much by human development, but that the WTR is regenerating after being partially deforested by Europeans. One clue to this deforestation is WTR's many pūkā plants. These are rare at the Almorah Road section. Pūkā is a sun-seeker, and commonly grows high up in the branches of other trees. But in the WTR, it grows on the ground. 'This suggests that there was plenty of light on the ground and few host trees when pūkā began to establish,' says Cameron. Another clue, pointed out by naturalist Jim Goulstone, is the WTR's lack of tiny native land snails, which are plentiful in nearby forest areas.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The first people to settle in the Mt Eden area were the Maori. Arriving in what is now the Auckland region around the 13th century, many tribes settled high up on the slopes of the volcano in Mt Eden specifically so they could defend themselves from enemies. Researchers believe Mt Eden's rock forests provided families with herbs, berries, bark and leaves. Some had nutritional value but could also be used to relieve pain and act as antiseptic. Legend has it that in the late 17th century, Mt Eden was declared tapu, that is, it became a place where people were forbidden to go. The community therefore relocated. When European settlers arrived in the 19th century, they saw resources in the rock forests like timber and rocks as ideal for new urban development, and used them as materials for housing, stores and gardens.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Nobody knows exactly how old the Mt Eden forest is, but it can't be older than the underlying lava rocks. The scientific method of carbon-dating suggests that the volcano in Mt Eden was erupting around 28,000 years ago; once the lava had cooled and broken up, it allowed plant life and eventually a forest to grow. But whereas we are able to track the development of tree species in other parts of Auckland, it can't be done in a rock forest. It is the analysis of historical pollen that allows scientists to carry out this kind of investigation, but rock forest conditions mean not enough pollen can be preserved.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The rock forest growing alongside Almorah Road was part of the grounds of a large property called Glade Hall. By 1999, the Hall had become run down and was put up for sale. Locals knew over half of the grounds were still covered by native forest, so when a developer offered to buy the property, on condition he could build 14 new houses, they quickly protested. They alerted Cameron, who pointed out the site's rarity to the Department of Conservation. Eventually, the department purchased it and turned it into a protected reserve.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Rock conservationists still face challenges. Unfortunately, the WTR and Almorah sites are continually under threat from weeds that crowd out true forest species. Possums and rats, animals not native to New Zealand, consume extraordinary quantities of vegetation and seeds, affecting the forest's ability to regenerate. Homeowners whose houses back onto the forest have also threatened its survival, despite being aware of the campaign to save it. Tree and rock removal and the dumping of garden waste have all threatened native plants. Fortunately, new regulations introduced by the council mean such behaviour can be prosecuted. And in early 2016, the council agreed to release funds to support a pest and weed eradication programme. This conservation programme has found early success in the surprise discovery of a small population of the fern Pellaea falcata, a plant in national decline. Cameron believes further discoveries are yet to be made.

content: The 0.7-hectare reserve is located in Mt Eden, Auckland. It has a number of native tree species, and it is noticeable how the {{19}} of these trees have developed and spread over the rocks. Because there is hardly any {{20}} in the forest, there is also a lack of water. According to botanist Ewen Cameron, nikau trees exist in the reserve because {{21}} have brought their seeds here. Cameron also says the reserve is different from other rock forests as its puka plants aren't growing in the usual way. This tells researchers that there was once more light reaching the earth, suggesting that European settlers had cut a number of trees down. According to Jim Goulstone, an absence of {{22}}, which are common in other rock forests, also suggests that Withiel went through a period of deforestation.
